I'm certainly not as plugged into the mammal world as I am to the bird world, so perhaps this isn't as unusual/interesting as it appears to be to me. Woodchucks breed once a year, during the late winter and spring months after the end of hibernation. Females give birth to 1-9 offspring about a month later, and they become independent after about two months. Woodchucks are considered sexually mature adults at 1-2 years old. This individual was likely an adult Woodchuck, as it was found on its own and seemed to be relatively large, probably within the 16-26 inch average adult length range. The sex of this Woodchuck was not able to be determined, as there is not much sexual dimorphism in the species except for that males tend to be larger than females. Woodchucks can be found in a wide variety of habitats including forests, fields, and meadows. Other organisms that may also live in these habitats include woody and herbaceous plants, insects, birds, squirrels, and deer. This individual was found in a grassy area next to a forest. A potential predator of this species is the Eastern Coyote (Canis latrans var.) and a potential source of prey is the Common Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale). •	Trophic level: Primary, secondary consumer
•	Description: Big, round, ground squirrels—unlike anything else nearby. Bushy tail and grayish-brown fur, often seen in open fields feeding on low plants. The most similar thing here is probably the muskrat, which is smaller, has a rat-like tail, and is always found near water.
•	Life Cycle: Groundhogs hibernate over winter, and breed upon emerging in March or April. Young are born after about a month and remain in their den until they develop their eyesight and fur. By the end of the summer, the family will scatter. 
•	Stage: This appears to be an adult, as in June a young one would probably be smaller. We saw this Groundhog several times living under the shed, but never saw signs of their being a family of them here. 
•	Sex: No easy way to determine.
•	Habitat: Open areas, often on forest edges. Hardly stray far from their burrows. Human development has allowed them to thrive. 
•	Predator: Red Foxes
•	Prey: low plants such as White Clover.

description: The American Beaver is a primary consumer. They are semi-aquatic, leaving the water to eat tree bark, roots, leaves, and wetland plants. Their most distinctive feature is their broad, flat, paddle-like tail which helps them swim. While not visible in this picture, the tail was present on this individual, identifying it as an American Beaver. They also have continuously growing front teeth, which must be kept in check through constant chewing, dexterous un-webbed front paws, and webbed hind feet. They are well adapted to life underwater with a transparent third eye membrane to allow them to see underwater, and the ability to seal off their nostrils and ears when submerged. One of their most well known behaviors is that they build lodges as shelters out of mud and sticks with underwater entrances. In some cases, they also build dams to create a deeper body of water where they can hide as protection from predators. They are monogamous, staying with the same breeding partner for multiple seasons. Females give birth to litters of 1-4kits after a gestational period of 3 months. Kits stay with their parents in the lodge for two years. They range all across the continental U.S. in ponds, rivers, and lakes. One potential predator is the bobcat (Lynx rufus), one potential competitor is the muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus), and a potential prey are aspen trees, specifically Populus tremuloides.

That is because this species not only hibernates through the winter months, but it estivates through the hottest months of the summer; they hibernate or estivate for ~7 months of the year. Mustang Island State Park

We parked near the entrance and this female ground squirrel unafraid of humans apparently begged for food. So we shared a few raw almonds. Spotted Ground Squirrel appears to have a shorter tail, like the one in these images, than that of Rio Grande Ground Squirrel. description:
Spermophile de Californie - Otospermophilus beecheyi - California ground squirrel

L'Écureuil terrestre (ou fouisseur) de Californie est une espèce de rongeurs de la famille des Sciuridés. Son nom latin commémore le naturaliste américain Frederick William Beechey.

Très présent dans l'ouest des États-Unis et du nord du Mexique, cet écureuil préfère les zones à végétation basse. 
Il creuse des terriers qui sont parfois occupés collectivement (mais chaque individu a sa propre entrée). 
Sa fourrure mouchetée, de gris, de brun clair et de poils sombres, lui offre un bon camouflage dans les rochers du littoral.  

Lorsqu'ils vivent en contact avec des humains, ces écureuils apprennent vite à venir chercher la nourriture offerte ou abandonnée par l'homme. 
Ce joli spécimen a posé pour moi près de la plage de Torrey Pines, San Diego, Californie, USA.

IDENTIFICATION
Ground squirrels are easily identified as they forage above ground near their burrows. The ground squirrel's body measures 9 to 11 inches and its semi-bushy tail adds another 5 to 9 inches in length. The fur is brownish gray and speckled with off-white along the back; the sides of the head and shoulders are light gray to whitish. One subspecies that occupies most of northern California has a dark, triangular-shaped patch on its back between the shoulders; this patch is missing from other species.
